title: What’s your favorite workflow to make highly polished animations with LLMs?
author: MrMortlocke
selftext:
I’ve been playing around with trying to create highly polished animations with mcp tools and I was wondering how you folks typically go about this. 

And I also had kinda kind of a strange idea.   
I have an old Xbox one Kinect sensor and an adapter for it to hook up to my desktop.

Think I could record my own body movements and convert that into nice, silky smooth animation for my character? Kinda like a jimmy rigged mocap studio. 

Idk. I’m just trying to think a little outside the box to help with my animation with games. Thoughts?

comments.author: SignificanceFun550
comments.body:
Ha.  Might work but video AI platforms generally have avatar mocap functions you could leverage directly instead.

I take an approach where I generate base plates with nanobanana and then use claude (or chatgpt codex, but tbh codex isnt as good at it) to render movements in python.

I can show you some examples:

[https://www.youtube.com/@JapanAlmanac](https://www.youtube.com/@JapanAlmanac)

100% of those videos use the approach I describe.  My best video using this approach got almost 9k views: [https://www.youtube.com/shorts/wtDfuMcT88Q](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/wtDfuMcT88Q)

comments.author: geanpn0
comments.body:
Honestly, I think the best animation pipeline right now is to take a few frames, ask Claude or Codex to generate specific frames or a reference image, and then use H3 MiniMax to generate a video.

That's the pipeline I'm currently using locally. I generate the video with H3 MiniMax, then run it through a system that converts the video into actual 3D animations.

It works incredibly well for pretty much any type of creature, and it's how I've created almost all the animations in my project. With a few small tweaks, I even managed to get it working for first-person animations.

I'll share a few example videos.

In game:

https://reddit.com/link/1xnohla/video/oq96aow3vlzh1/player

All of this was AI-generated. The entire video, all the climbing and descending animations, the horse running, walking, the transitions, literally everything.

The whole pipeline runs locally. The only thing I actually paid for was a few minor corrections claude had to make to the starting and ending frames. But once you have the base, everything becomes much easier.

I run everything on my AMD RX 9070 XT, but I've also started using Google Colab. With a subscription costing around $18 USD, you can generate roughly 600 videos like this.

replies.author: geanpn0
replies.body:
Here's a zombie staggering animation. It took four 1-second iterations, mainly because of the limited screen space available for movement.

By combining three of those clips and asking the AI to adjust only the starting and ending frames of each one, I managed to get an almost perfect zombie stagger.

I'm not going to use this particular animation in my game, but it turned out pretty damn cool!

https://reddit.com/link/1xnohla/video/8s9thaz6vlzh1/player

replies.author: IndividualGain1836
replies.body: How do you generate an identical video in multiple orientations

replies.author: geanpn0
replies.body:
Basically, you start with a reference image showing the character from two angles: a front view and a side view. You can also do this directly in Blender and ask Claude to automate the whole process. You can even use my image as a reference.

For something like a horse, which is a well-known animal with a very recognizable movement pattern, the simplest approach is to just provide the reference image and ask the AI to animate it. For example, "a horse running." That's exactly what I did with the horse in my pipeline.

The zombie animation is a bit more complicated. I provide five keyframes, and H3 MiniMax actually supports using multiple frames as references, generating the animation between them.

Each frame is just an image showing both the front and side views of the character, side by side. That's also why you need to leave enough space in the frame for the character to move without going out of bounds.

Each image represents a different part of the movement: the beginning, middle, end, and so on. Then you simply ask H3 MiniMax to fill in the gaps and generate the transitions.

The cool thing is that even if you know how to animate, creating smooth, natural-looking movement is incredibly difficult. Whether it's a human, a zombie, or an animal, there's a lot more to making something feel alive than just moving its legs.

That's why I find it much easier to guide the AI by creating keyframes that represent the movement I want, and then let MiniMax handle the interpolation and all the little details. It's surprisingly good at understanding and completing those movements.

I've also tested Google's Gemini, Nano Banana for image generation, and Omni for video generation, but they didn't work nearly as well for this. They just don't follow the instructions consistently enough.

For me, this video generation and interpolation pipeline is by far the most useful approach I've found.

So ideally, you either run the whole thing locally on your own PC or use Google Colab to run MiniMax for video generation.

replies.author: IndividualGain1836
replies.body:
I've got the generation element I believe the issue seems to be tracking it to my Skeleton, even with Dyno Claude seems to struggle with making it natural. How could I move this to local without Claude? 

How also can I get the skeleton to track smoothly like yours does?

replies.author: IndividualGain1836
replies.body:
Example top is generated video and here is Dyno trying to track a simple wood chop

https://i.redd.it/ziuseeq81ozh1.gif

replies.author: geanpn0
replies.body:
This happened to me a lot too, especially with my initial pipeline when I was trying to adapt it from humanoids to horses. It's something you'll have to work through with Claude and gradually refine.

Since I have a programming background, I was able to implement some constraints to minimize these issues.

What I'd recommend is asking Claude to implement joint rotation limits and use both camera views with variable weights depending on the animation and character.

In your case, for example, your character seems to be standing at an angle rather than facing directly forward. You can see that the left leg and left arm are barely visible from the side camera, so the system needs to rely more heavily on the front camera to reconstruct those movements correctly.

These weights need to be adjusted depending on the character. A horse, for example, requires completely different joint constraints and weighting. You need to tell Claude to account for the actual anatomy and biomechanics of a quadruped. If it applies the same constraints and weights used for a human, you'll run into exactly these problems, because the legs move differently and have different ranges of motion.

Once you've established those constraints, there's honestly not much else you can do without deeper technical knowledge besides iterating with Claude and fixing issues as they appear.

Eventually, you'll end up with a pipeline that works consistently across different videos and characters, which is where I'm at now.

Also, it's not that my animations magically came out smooth. I generated them using carefully planned keyframes with very specific timing for each movement.

For example, with your attack animation, I'd recommend keeping the entire attack under one second.

Usually, DINO doesn't fail at tracking. What DINO does is identify the skeleton, and it's generally pretty accurate at that.

If you ask Claude to generate a visualization video showing DINO's tracking results, you'll probably see that the tracking itself is almost perfect.

What usually fails is the converter Claude built to map DINO's output onto your actual character skeleton, since they're two different skeleton structures.

That's why it's really useful to have a video showing DINO's tracking results. You can use it to point out to Claude that the issue is actually in the second stage, the skeleton conversion, rather than the tracking itself.

Once Claude can see that DINO's skeleton tracking is correct, it can usually identify the problem and adjust the conversion accordingly.

comments.author: FragmentedHeap
comments.body:
I built software from scratch that sits on top comfyui and I put flow ts on pi inside of it so app has its own agent. 

Then I built features for 2d character poses, that then run through pixel3d and hi3d refiner. 

And then I built another workflow that actually builds a human being from a real human skeleton all the way up to the ligaments and muscles in organs and skin. 

And then I built a harness so that my agent and side of the application can generate this character for me run it through the mesh refiner and then grow a human skeleton inside of it until it molds to and replaces the original high 3D mesh. 

And what comes out of the other end is a fully polished 3D model where I can move everything down to a finger joint. 

Then I run that through nvidias new animation ai to animate it. 

Then it gets exported at lower detail. 


Then it's ready to use in my custom engine. 

Used AI to make everything, even my text renderer. 

Im doing the same thing for audio, music, animations, movies, etc. 

I built this awesome software that can do this and then I go into it and I sign into openai and I let Astra drive it directly. 

So I said no to the mCP tools and instead I built a harness inside of my software that the AI can use directly. 

I'm not using artificial intelligence to make a game. 

I'm using artificial intelligence to build the studio and the pipeline that I then put artificial intelligence inside of that then makes the game.

I'm basically trying to take every production pipeline that's ever exist and shove it inside of here and then teach AI how to drive it on its own.

My end goal is to walk away from unreal engine and blender and all of those tools including FL studio and so on entirely 

And end up with one piece of software where everything is one complete whole that AI is sitting inside of

And I went all the way down to the bones. 

I built a multi-channel sign distance field text rendering engine from scratch that allows me to take any standard font and turn it into a 3D asset and draw with it in the game. 

Where each individual character and side of the font is animatable. 

I can render a text editor on water and that's already working. 

And my sound studio is going to be able to compose music down to the musical sheet and hook up all the instruments and play it.

Using eleven labs to make new instruments

Basically I decided that trying to get an existing coding harness to do all of this with a bunch of mCP tools was really inefficient and what everybody else was doing. 

So I just decided to rebuild the software from the ground up and make it AI native

If I succeed I'll be able to make things really quickly and I won't be paying licensing to anybody not even unreal engine.

And I've taken great care to make sure that anything I touch is either commercially legal or MIT.

I'm in the middle of recreating everything on top of rust, c, c++, and using it all of in a new engine built in csharp, aot compat, and optimized heavily.

The final engine will run on all three major operating systems natively and produce games for all three major operating systems natively. 

I currently have no plans to support consoles.

comments.author: ImCallingYouOutOnBS
comments.body: Honestly, the approach I've been taking is training Claude on my own art. I draw something animated in 2D, have it go frame by frame, and have it make a lessons.md and it adds more and more to it until it copies my art style exactly
